Title: Ian Forestal--the Busiest Man in Show Business

Messages.Author: Shawn F. Carnes
Messages.Body:
Lots o' interesting discussions on this card. First, I will leak
that his blood cap. is 8, not the 7 of the playtest cards. His
ability of every minor discipline stayed.

My take on it is this--it is *not* broken; it is a strong card, but
not broken. First off, he's an 8 blood vampire. To bring him in
takes optimally 2 solid rounds of transfers, and still 2 rounds with
Info. Highway. At the start of a game, it is usually three unless you
have an optimal start at 4 transfers.

Next, his two key disciplines are auspex and dominate (ones that cross
over potentially with other clans). Thaumaturgy is a sole primary of
the Tremere, so of course you might include him in a Tremere deck.
Auspex and Dominate mesh well with Malkavian, fairly well with Toreador
and Ventrue. Still, an 8 blood vampire only has the basic level
disciplines associated with the clan Ian will work with. I don't think
that it is that major. Strong, yes, but not broken.

He also doesn't have a title. Yes, he can get one, but an 8 blood vamp
not having a title is harsh. Chances are he won't be in a vote deck.
Finally--if he is popular, I expect to see him contested like nobody's
business.

That's my opinion. Take it for what it is worth.
--

Rebekka (TRE 8 AUS pot PRE THA -- +1 stealth; +1 bleed vs. MAL)

The vampires all have decent abilities that are well within point range.
Just because I might not use Corneluis's Quietus, however, doesn't mean I
shouldn't have to pay for it.

The whole "you won't use all the abilities" is a null-argument. Use is

since they don't use all those disciplines.

> Chances are he won't be in a vote deck.

> business.

paraphrasing): "Democritus at 6 pool would be too good. Just because a
card will be contested, that doesn't mean it will be balanced."

The fix of this card is easy. Change it so that Ian is able to play
cards of disciplines he doesn't have as though he had inferior, but _NOT_
(!!!!) that playing the first skill card raises him to superior. (Thus,
playing an Animalism on him would give him inferior, and a Second one
would give him superior.

> That's my opinion. Take it for what it is worth.

This one isn't worth too much. The card is a travesty.

[Off Topic notes] <SkinOfSteel=ON>

Ancient Hearts was a good step in the right direction after (the horrid)
Dark Sovereigns and the (near total) bungling of the 2nd Printing of
V:TES. Why does it seem that Jyhad's current designers are determined to
wreck a good thing?

Shawn, I know this is harsh, but I have not been happy with the steps
I've seen you taking. TTBOMK, under you, Jyhad has been stumbling down a
slope towards breaking, with only a slight stall at Ancient Hearts. One
of the great features of (the original) Jyhad is the economy of its cards:
each thing has a cost appropriate to the card. This principle seems to
be disappearing under you. I used to say to people, "Jyhad is the most
balanced game on the market..." I am beginning to fear I may no longer
say this.

On this newsgroup, a lot of people are relatively fanatical about this
game. It is excellent, and far better than anything else I've seen on
the market. However, the nature of the CCG is that the balance of power
changes with new cards. For the most part, I have seen Jyhad's balance
becoming more and more tenuous (though still holding), and I hope this
trend won't continue. This balance is what (I think) maintains fans to
Jyhad. Most people I know who get into Jyhad, stay into Jyhad (barring
RL forcing them to stop playing games). Don't toss out your core
supporters by hurting this game any more.

I apologize if that is harsh. All I know is that at every convention,
tournament, game group I have been at, 95% of the players I have talked
to have been concerned about where Jyhad is heading. Ancient Hearts
perked most of us up (with a few singular card exceptions), but we're
still wary. Don't disappoint us. There are so few good games out there,
it'd be a shame if this ceases to be one.

Well, that would make him a _little_ bit better, but it is still
a two point power to gain every discipline in the game. 21 for 8 is
still the best trade in the game. He should have some restrictions,
such as spending blood to use disciplines he doesn't have, or that no
master skills may be placed on him.

> My take on it is this--it is *not* broken; it is a strong card, but

> Info. Highway. At the start of a game, it is usually three unless you

Does the number of transfers it takes to bring him out really
matter? A degenerate card is a degenerate card no matter how long it
takes to bring him out or how many people contest him.

> Next, his two key disciplines are auspex and dominate (ones that cross

> and Ventrue. Still, an 8 blood vampire only has the basic level

Why is he *this* strong? Why doesn't he get his powers the way
other vampires do, by paying for them?

> He also doesn't have a title. Yes, he can get one, but an 8 blood vamp

> not having a title is harsh. Chances are he won't be in a vote deck.

No? With basic presence and Dominate, and Auspex, he's very good
in a reactive or active vote deck. Telepathic Vote Counting, Kindred
Coercion, Pulling Strings, Dread Gaze, Treachery, Bewitching Oration-
plus new cards from the Sabbat. Make him a Ventrue, and he can Elder
Kindred Network and really hurt your opponent.
Bindusara has no title-a 9 cap. Ventrue, at that. Neither does:
Rebekka, Cornelius Ottavio, Makarios, Ebenezer Roush, and all of
the non-Cam 8 and above (that's votes, not title). Compared to an extra
_few_ points in disciplines, Forestal is still better in the long run
than Tura Vaughn, who has a title.
Someone commented that the weakness of the Tremere was their
inability to vote. That hasn't been fixed (except by making a Tremere
immune to Bloodhunts) just like Gangrel vote hasn't been fixed. The
Tremere have just been made better fighters and bleeders. I could have
seen a Thaumaturgy reaction/action modifier based off the Path of
Corruption that could have changed votes from no to yes(action) &
yes to no (reaction), instead of a broken hoser.
However, the Tremere still have more Princes than the Gangrel
and Malkavians, and as many as the Nosferatu. What's the difference?
The Tremere have bigger Princes with better powers; compare Nikolaus
Vermeulen to Javier Montoya, and compare Murat to Spiridonas. Why
weren't these clans made better bleeders and fighters, or given
overpowered vampires?

> Finally--if he is popular, I expect to see him contested like nobody's
> business.

See above. If everyone's contesting *Death Ray* Forestal
because he's so much better than everybody else, it means that he was
made with more powers and fewer drawbacks than anybody else. Why?
Is there a problem with the Tremere in the basic set that had
to be fixed by giving them cards like the Ankara Citadel, and vampires
like Spiridonas, Muaziz, Rebekka, Kalinda, Parnassus, and Ian? Even
before DS, the Tremere were a good clan. Look at Merill Molitor,
Chantry, Arcane Library(one of only three).

> That's my opinion. Take it for what it is worth.

And this is mine. Ian Forestal is a broken card, not worthy of
inclusion in the Sabbat. The point system that evens out vampire
abilities had been cracked with Rebekka, broken with Muaziz, and Ian
Forestal takes a hammer to the remnants. Jyhad/V:teS appears to be
slowly weighted to some clans and some cards, and I, for one, do not
wish to play a broken game simply because it was good once.
There are other vampires (Tremere, undoubtedly) of Ian's
caliber, I assume, and that frightens me. Blythe wasn't really a
misprint, was she?? She was a playtest version who wasn't changed..
I don't think that we'll see any other overpowered vampires before
the Sabbat comes out, will we? Not with our adamant stand against
Ian...

points. And, frankly, vampires so large almost always waste disciplines,

Well, the people who designed the other 8+ blood vampires apparently
thought that the vampire should pay for the inferior disciplines:
Crusher pays full price for inferior fortitude.
Don Cruez pays full price for inferior ani, dom, and pro
Miranda Pays an extra half point (3.5) for her three inferior skills.
(probably due to rounding the "Primogen" half point.)
Tura pays full price for inferior dominate.
Angus pays an extra half point (3.5) for his three inferior skills.
Dr. Jest pays full price for his *4* inferior skills.

So why not have Ian pay a minimum of three points for his 14+ inferior skills?
That's certainly a precedent set way back in 1994. Paying four would
not be out of line, and would make him balanced with the likes of Dr.J

Two is unthinkable, unless you also reduce Angus to a 9 capacity, Don Cruez
to a 9, etc. (paying two for three unneeded skills is certainly at least
as balanced as paying two for *all* unneeded skills).

>He also doesn't have a title. Yes, he can get one, but an 8 blood vamp
>not having a title is harsh. Chances are he won't be in a vote deck.

He doesn't pay for a title. Not having a title/skill/ability that you
don't pay for in not harsh - ask Rebekka.

Being handed a pack of skills that you haven't paid for is harsh for
the competitors - which is why Anvil always seems to come out once
a game.

>Finally--if he is popular, I expect to see him contested like nobody's
>business.

Then why not leave Blythe's auspex at superior? She'd be overwhelmingly
great (like Ian is now) and everyone would contest her. You fixed it
then because it was broken, even though the contesting "check/balance"
would have curtailed her runaway use. Fix Ian now, instead of using the
uniqueness factor as a crutch.

sounded too harsh. Unfortunately, I cannot word it much differently...]

The idea that the work the design team has done has been good for the
game is highly debatable. If the design team is also the rules team,
then it is highly laughable. In a fluctuating game like a CCG, there
come times when a ruling or bring about a new card type will set the game
down a path. At these junctures, multiple avenues are available, but
once a road is chosen, it's hard to retrace steps (the cards are out
there, after all). It seems every time the design team / rules team has
an opportunity to go down a bad path, they take it, be it with the
overkill on anti-bleed cards in the V:tES reprinting, the total lack of
design savvy with Dark Sovereigns, the leaning towards Tremere as of
late, rulings on Clan Impersonation (which someone override card text
despite not having any card text that would make this apparent from the
card), and many other examples.

Sadly, I am not the only one of this opinion.

Shawn, you may be in a unique position to change this. Really, there are
only a few simple rules that need be followed:
1) Cards should have an appropriate card cost (either
pool/blood/discipline/etc.)
2) "Trump" cards should not be made (clarification: a Brujah frenzy
hinders Brujah, but doesn't trump Brujah as Archon Investigation does)
3) Cards should be appropriate to the group using them (Ian Forestal's
ability is appropriate for Tremere (though not expensive enough) though
not Nossies)

There are far more subtle things that are important, but cost,
appropriateness to the game world, and making cards that advance
strategies rather than trump them are the important things.

It seems the Design Team has forgotten that.

First: Perhaps a blanket brush-off is too harsh, without supporting evidence.
In fact, that’s probably what you see the above as. However, when one looks at
things from the perspectives of the people who have been posting about game
balance and Ian recently, one will find that we do have a point.

Our evidence and points? I e-mailed a letter with my arguments about the
Tremere being overpowered and helped out too much in AH to you earlier this
month, Shawn. You may not have gotten it; if so, send me mail and I’ll send you
another copy. In that letter, I made the same point about Ian Forestal which I
and others have made on the newsgroup, and also discussed each of the Tremere
cards which I and others percieve as evidence of a bias on the design team’s
part towards the Tremere.

The primary problem which I have(and this goes for a number of other people, I
know) with certain Tremere and Thaumaturgy cards and Dark Soveriegns in
particular, is that the cards tend to fit into two categories, with very few in
the middle: underpowered/too expensive(most of DS library cards with a few
exceptions, and a number of 5 and 6 capacities from both expansions who are
clearly undercosted in most analyses of the point creation system) and
overpowered/too inexpensive(most of the ‘spoiler’ cards which people complain
about, the two large AH Tremere, and to a lesser extent, the Inner Circle
members). The underpowered cards are almost useless, and various proposed
“fixes” have sprung up to solve the fact that it is almost worthless to play
them as written. The overpowered cards, although they may not break or throw
the game all on their own(with the exception of Spiridonas, who has swept tables
around here in a Malk/Tremere Stealth and Bleed deck) are a dangerous sign of
what might be coming in the next expansion set; and when I saw Ian Forestal in
the duelist, it seemed as if my worst fears(and those of others) had been
completely validated: that not only had the design team not recognized the cards
that had been put out as unbalanced, but that they were going to create cards
which were even MORE unbalanced.

My main concern is that Jyhad stays the best CCG on the market. Its system was
based on a solid foundation of rules and mechanics which keep all strategies
relatively equal in power, and no card necessarily better than another. All
this changed when V:tES came out, and new cards were introduced which hosed
bleed for no apparent reason. Not only did these cards hose bleed(Archon
Investigation, Protected Resources, and to a lesser extent, Justicar
Retribution) but they also were GENERIC hosers that anyone could use without any
thought required to make them work. As such, bleed’s ability to function as a
viable strategy took a huge dive as long as those cards were legal and
available; and bleed is usually very vulnerable to rush, vote, and intercept.
The cards solved a ‘problem’ which wasn’t there.

Dark Soveriegns introduced very few cards which could be considered to be
spoilers...but it also introduced very little that could be considered anything
else, either. The high point of DS was the Inner circlers and the other
vampires with too many points for their capacity(Blythe Candeleria, even with
the errata, and Francois Villon); these were disturbing, but tended to balance
out due to the large investment needed to use most of them effectively.
However, the fact that there were vampires in the same expansion who were
underpowered(at least the two 5 capacity non-cams, Sigrid Bekker, Darius Styx
after the D action ruling, and Teresa Rostas) was, if possible, more disturbing.
It seemed as if the point system, which worked reasonably well to balance
vampires in the basic set, had been thrown out the window, without any simple
guidelines as to what was under or over powered.

This impression was only reinforced by Ancient Hearts. All the 6 capacity
vampires in AH were under-costed for their disciplines, titles, and powers. The
most that any of their powers could be realistically construed as would be a
point for Nakova, and that would make her have 4 and 1/2 points for 6 capacity;
an identical deal to Judah and Elizabetha Romano. Damaskenos was the best of
those vampires at 5 for 6, and I still have not been able to find a use for him
where someone else could be better. Muaziz and Spiridonas, on the other hand,
struck me as overpowered the moment I saw them. Muaziz pays 2 points for her +1
stealth and immunity to bloodhunts; whereas in the basic set, Lucretia paid two
points for her +1 stealth alone. Not only that, but Muaziz was the 2nd Tremere
with +1 stealth, the first being Rebekka from DS, who only escapes the list of
overpowered vampires by being difficult to integrate into most decks. Even so,
she is on the high end of reasonable; and Muaziz is over the top, even if she
won’t break a game all on her own. Spiridonas, if he can get through, is a
monster, who can get up to +7 bleed from his special ability alone. Not having
blood is a problem? C’mon. He’s a Tremere, a member of the clan which regains
blood the fastest in the Game. And he can always use hospitality on himself.

Get the idea yet? Do our concerns strike you as totally unfounded now, Shawn?

I have the highest respect for the design team at WotC; but I’m extremely
frightened by the idea that I might have a clearer grasp on the basic system for
powering vampires and library cards than they do. The only reason that I have
that idea at all are the (multiple) vampires who don’t have their points in
abilities and the number of points they should have match, and the various cards
which I’ve seen come out recently which strike me as spoilers. I do not believe
that we are just brushing these people off; we are concerned that they might be
doing things which will adversely affect a game which we love and are somewhat
fanatical about, and as such, we WILL do our damndest to try to communicate our
concerns to them(through you, as you are the only person on the team who we have
any way of communcating with at all).

If you and the design team desire to make the best TCG possible, as I believe
that you do, then that goal would likely be aided by listening to those players
who actually care about the balance and equity of the game when they express
concerns about the power and/or inconsistency of a card as compared to the cards
from the original set and the other expansions. We have no way of even making
sure that you listen to us, much less consider what we’re saying. If you find
our concerns ungrounded, then please explain to us in a cogent, cohesive
argument why you find them so, without resorting to arguments which have been
overturned earlier out of common sense, consistency, or whatever. I do not mean
to be offensive; I just found your justification of Ian extremely weak(as I’m
sure you know by now).

I, myself, will do almost anything to try to keep Jyhad the best TCG possible.
If I can communicate with the people in R&D about my concerns, I will. If I
have to playtest for no pay, I will. If I have to rant on the net about how
unbalanced certain cards in previous and the next expansions are until people
pay attention, I will.

There are two main points which I want to get across with this
post/letter; all of the above will have been wasted bandwidth if these are
ignored. One is that I and almost every other player on this group would like
Jyhad to be the best balanced, high quality, interesting game it can be, and to
avoid from stepping into the realms of overpowered and unbalanced cards which
EVERY other TCG that I’ve seen (except possibly Netrunner) has entered. We care
about the game, and as such, are not simply rabid maniacs trying to change
something on a whim. I’ve seen more posts on Ian than I’ve seen on almost any
other topic, ever. When the players, especially those who debate the balance
and theory of the game for hours and months on end, are concerned about
something, it would be good for the netrep or game company representative to(at
the absolute least) listen to their concerns and bring them up.

The second point is that there seems to be very little communication seems to
occur between the people at WotC and the players of Jyhad/V:tES. The only
person who we have access to is the Netrep, who will not necessarily see every
post or respond to every concern due to time constraints and other aspects of
his job. When we find something to be a major issue of concern, very little or
nothing is typically done about it; whether this is a matter of Jyhad’s lesser
clout at WotC or just a lack of importance placed on Jyhad’s players is
debatable. But we do not get our voices through, or heard at all, from all of
the evidence that I’ve seen.

This lack of communication can be dealt with. Would it be so hard to discuss
issues of game balance and design with us? I, for one, don’t think that it
would be. Is it the most important part of your job to be talking to players
about game balance? Obviously not. Would it help iron out the often major
discrepancies between what players think is reasonable and what WotC thinks is
reasonable? Absolutely. It would also create an enviroment in which the
players and the people in charge of the game would be able to work together to
make Jyhad not just the best TCG on the market, but possibly the best TCG ever.

Alec Chang, Concerned Gamer and advocate for better communications between WotC
and their consistuents(customers, I mean).

Messages.Author: CurtAdams
Messages.Body:
"Shawn F. Carnes" <sw...@castle.wizards.com> writes:

>The
>people with whom I work on V:TES are a dedicated core group of people
>who have every committment to making the best TCG possible. I know *FOR
>A FACT* that we have no desire to "mirror" M:tG, and such an assumption
>is false.

It's inapproriate to accuse you or any other member of the VtES design
team of ill-will towards Jyhad/V:tES, or of an obsession with Magic.
Newsgroups are firey places; don't take personal attacks seriously,
although pointing out personal attacks as such is often a good idea. But,
you should know, when Dark Sovereigns came out, the only disagreement in
my group was whether to call it "Vampire: the Gathering" or "Magic with
Fangs".

When Jyhad came out it had many things that distinguished it from Magic,
including an absence of a lot of elements common in Magic. Jyhad players
assumed that these distinctions were mostly based on things that, while
perhaps cute or initially appealing, were a bad thing for Magic. Amongst
these were:

1) Very few cards with global effects.
2) Significant unique restrictions on many desired cards (e.g. Master
locations)
3) Very few cards with unlimited effects, especially "pay X for X".
4) A marked preference for simple cards requiring combinations over
complex standalone cards.
5) An absence of built-in antipathies (e.g. clan vs. clan)
6) Few cards that mucked with the game mechanics, with the ones that did
mild.

Exceptions to the above rules basically came only from votes and Malkavian
cards. Even there, exceptions were few.

Dark Sovereigns came out breaking of the above, in spades. I'd say more
than half of the cards in DS broke at least one of the above rules. Some
were wallpaper, a few spoilers, but even when neither, they just didn't
look or feel like Jyhad cards. "All Gangrel gain +1 hand damage" was the
kind of effect you just didn't see in Jyhad, for *any* cost. In Jyhad,
you had a card the *one* Gangrel could use for 2 hand damage, and that
didn't do any good if they already had 2 hand. DS cards, as a whole,
differ significantly from Jyhad cards, and basically they always differ by
being more like Magic.

I don't think this is *deliberate*, but I do believe that most of the
Design Team are Magic players who were assigned to Jyhad/V:tES. Hence I
do think V:tES is being "Magicized", albeit unintentionally.

To clarify where people are coming from, you should remember that people
who play Jyhad/V:tES usually dislike Magic. If you like Magic, you play
Magic. Jyhad/V:tES does have aspects that make it better for multiplayer
play, but people don't appreciate them unless they play Jyhad quite a bit,
and they're unlikely to do that unless they've soured on Magic. So when
you make V:tES more like Magic (and you have) you are damaging or even
destroying the game for these folks (most Jyhad/V:tES players).

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)

> > Also, I would be interested, in general, how the Netizens of this

> > group analyze the design of a vampire.

Well, it just got figured out. It's easy to see that disciplines are
worth 1 "unit". For example, look at all of the 4 capacity vampires
without special abilities. They _all_ have 3 "units"; 3 disciplines or
2, with one at superior. Also, a master: discipline card gives a
vampire +1 capacity. So, we would think about how to build up a vampire
from scratch using printed cards. From there, it's (relatively) easy to
see the rest.

So...

Point System:

A vampire gets a certain number of points, based on capacity:

Capacity Points
1-3 Cap-1
4-8 Cap
9+ Cap+1

Points can be "spent" as follows:
1 pt. -- Inferior discipline
2 pts. -- Superior discipline
2 pts. -- Either +1 bleed or +1 hand damage
1 pt. -- Title (any)

Special abilities. These can vary, and usually cost more the better
they are. Also, "defects". These count as negative points, because
they make the vampire worse. This is how Caitiff can have disciplines.
Also, some specials cost zero, usually when they are clan-specific.

Here are examples from my favorite clan, the Gangrel:

Giuliano "Diablerie" Vincenzi
Capacity 2 --> 1 Point: for (1)

Anastasia Grey
Capacity 3 --> 2 Points: pro ani (2)

Chandler Hungerford
Capacity 3 --> 2 points: PRO (2), +1 int. v. Gangrel (0)

Zack North
Capacity 6 --> 6 points: pot for pro ani (4), +1 hand damage (2)

Gitane St. Claire
Capacity 7 --> 7 points: ANI FOR PRO (6), Primogen (1)

Gunther -- Beast Lord
Capacity 7 --> 7 points: aus pro for ANI (5), Pay 1 blood to untap at
end of your turn (Special). Either Gunther is over priced, or his
ability is actually worth 2 points (I'm inclined toward the former).

Quinton McDonnell
Capacity 8 --> 8 points: cel ani pro FOR (5), Primogen (1), +1 hand
damage (2)

-----
That's it. It works for most vampires, and it tells us when vampires
are overpriced (like Radeyah, an AH Toreador with 4 pts. of disciplines
and a clan-specific ability) and lets us be outraged by the un-errata-ed
Blythe Candeleria and Ian Forestal.

Fellow Players and Our Net-rep,

I think I may have added to some confusion when, in my posts, I referred
to Ian Forestal as a broken card. That is not a correct statement and I
used the term thoughtlessly. As others have pointed out, the feeling
seems to be that the card is underpriced for what it does.

I don't feel, nor have I read in these threads, that Ian Forestal will
break the game. I do think that substantially underpricing a vampire is
unfair and a bad idea.

To be sure, there are other vampires from the basic set that have all of
their clan's basic disciplines at superior for 8 cost (e.g. Tura Vaughan,
Ebanezer Roush) or even 7 cost (Gilbert Duane, Sir Walter Nash, Gitane St.
Claire.) These vampires are just as apporopriate and useful as Ian
Forestal for building a crypt based on their clans' three disciplines.
Some of them even have useful titles or powers. So far, so good.

But when building decks with skills added in beyond the basic disciplines,
those other vampires are generally less useful as they would now probably
require a master skill to be able to use the entire library. Or they
could be dropped for costlier vampires that may have the needed skills.
Ian Forestal doesn't have that problem.

Whatever deck concept the player wants his Tremere deck to have, Ian will
fit right in. Add in celerity? Use Ian. Need some Presence? Try Ian.
How about putting in some Fortitude? Ian will work. He can and will be
used by every Tremere deck that wants to add in a discipline, I imagine.
I don't see him being contested as much as has been hinted though. Would
the Ventrue deck have need of an 8 capacity with only Dominate at
superior? Do Brujah want an 8 cost vamp with no superiors? How would an
8 capacity, ani for pro, vamp help the Gangrel?

This vamp will only work truly well for the Tremere, and the Malks
somewhat, giving them a greater flexibility in adding disciplines to the
clan mix. I imagine that he would be rarely if ever seen in any other
clan's crypt. For them he would be an 8 cost untitiled vamp with 3 or 4
points of useful skills. Hardly a world beater.

What I'm trying to get at is that while I don't think having Ian Forestal
in your crypt gives you an advantage during the game, I _do_ believe that
having Ian Forestal as an option for your crypt increases the number of
discipline combinations you can use and so increases the versatility and
range of strategies of a Tremere crypt. No other clan has a
one-size-fits-all vamp like Ian. (And I _don't_ want every other clan to
get a vamp just like Ian. That is not a solution.)

Hope this comes across clear. I'm not certain that my arguement is stated
as well as it might be. Please feel free to ask me if something is fuzzy.

Keeping an eye on the moon,
Doug Dunaway

Vampire stealing is also (virtually) a non-issue. The only ways a

Cap 2 DOM OBF +1 bleed

Cap 5 AUS CEL PRE +1 intercept on all actions

like( insert your personal list here; I've got mine) Muaziz, Spiridonas, Archon
Investigation, Thoughts Betrayed, The Tomb of Rameses, etc....

Basically, the point is not and would never be that Ian will completely dominate
the game; there is too much variety in deck construction for that to ever happen.
What I (at least) am saying, is that the distinction between Ian 'having' all the
disciplines and 'haivng a special power which lets him use all the disciplines' is
moot. There is only one card in the entire game which will hinge in it's
functionality on that distinction. That's all. In all other ways, Ian can be
considered to have gotten 14 points in disciplines for two points.

Or, if you want to look at it another way, Ian pays 8 for 20 points in disciplines.
That comes out to 2.5 points in disciplines per point spent by the vampire. So,
now I can pay (4 for 10 points in disciplines, 2 for +2 bleed, 2 for Inner Circle,
0 for special ability=8) only 8 pool for Arika, bringing her out my second turn,
and Bleeding my prey to pieces. And if I can't, by Ian's standard(which had damn
well not become the norm in any way), all other vampires are outdated,
underclassed, and a great deal of them are rendered obselete. Except for cards
which were mistakes in the first place, this game should not be making anything
obselete or useless. Raven, the only vampire to be replaced, IS Camille Devereaux.
This should say something; namely, that the vampires in the basic set were made
along distinctly drawn and very balanced lines. Ian, and a growing number of
vampires in the expansions, are not.

Messages.Author: James Puzzo
Messages.Body:
Malcolm McCallum (mcca...@pacificcoast.net) wrote:
: People seem to be looking at this in a skewed manner. When a vampire is
: dropped into a deck, he is put in for his special abilities or his
: disciplines.

True. And Ian has every discipline.

: In all the decks that I've ever seen, 3 disciplines are all
: that are used.

In decks that _you've_ seen. First off, I have seen effective decks using
more than 3 disciplines. Secondly, with vampires like Ian (I see him as
setting a disturbing precedent) these multi-discipline decks become far more
easy to pull off.

: To try to use 4 is to risk not getting the correctly disciplined
: vampires out.

If you get Ian out, you have no worries. Put three of him in a crypt of
12 and you're relatively certain you'll get him. At a cost of 8, you get
assurance AND versatility for quite a low cost. Hmmm.

: Ian may change this, especially if there are other vampires coming
: out with related abilities, but I expect not.

I think you underestimate the power of precedent if you do not think that
these underpriced vampires will become more common. And his existence has
already changed the balance by making these multi-discipline focus decks
more workable.

: Don't think of Ian as having every discipline.

Aside from the fact that he actually has every discipline, is there a good
reason not to? :(

: Think of him as having only those disciplines that you want for your
: deck because that is the only way that the cost matters.

But the fact that the SAME vampire can be used in MULTIPLE discipline
strategies would seem to me to make him _more_ valuable.

: Also, it is not a card that specifically benefits Tremere.

Whether it benefits the Tremere or not is moot. I argue against the precedent
of severely underpricing a minion.

: If anything, it hoses them a bit.

Pray tell.

: For example, I can now think about including Ian in my Giovanni deck
: since he has obfuscate, dominate, and necromancy. As well, I can
: throw in some tremere sites. The effect of this is to increase the

: liklihood that the Tremere will be contested.

So the Tremere aren't especially happy. But think of it from the Giovanni
side... they now have the ability to use a vampire with all of their
disciplines at inferior... PLUS the ability to utilize (or contest!!) unique
Tremere locations, etc. The fact that he can be utilized as a Tremere
hozer AND can be used effectively in any discipline strategy should increase
his value.

: Here's another take: *Because* he can use any ability, Ian will be the
: vampire most likely to be targetted for take over by your opponent and
: when he is taken, he will be more of a boon to your opponent than any
: other vampire. Therefore, should his cost not be less? He is a liability.

The likelyhood of contestation should NOT _decrease_ the value of ANYTHING.
If anything, this likelyhood indicates that a resource is quite valuable
indeed. I argue that such a valuable resource (which is SO likely to be
contested) should cost more in the first place. To state that a truly prized
possession should be undervalued because many others will want it seems
to be counter-intuitive.

: Also, I am not fond of the 'point system' argument. From a purely players

: point of view, there is no point system.

How about a game background argument? That a Tremere whose special skills
seem to be related to arcane matters should cost him blood?

How about the contestation argument? That a card that appears to be a highly
contestable is probably undervalued?

: It ain't in the rules.

Finally, there is nothing in the rules that states that there can't
be a card which states: "Unique Master. When played, the playing Meth's
prey is immediately ousted. The playing Meth. gains ALL of the prey's pool,
as well as the bonus for ousting his prey". However, the fairness of this
card with respect to card balance and game mechanics is suspect, wouldn't
you say? The DESIGN of the game is not solely based on the rule set. The
PLAY of the game is. I question the DESIGN of Ian. That is INDEPENDENT of
the rules.

: As soon as every character starts fitting neatly into a formula the
: game will become equally as formulaic.

And as soon as every character is overpowered and underpriced the game will
no longer be Jyhad, which was one of the few games which exhibited careful
thought for game balance.

: Sit back. Chill out. Have some faith.

I've been sitting back. I'm about as chilled as I can be. The faith bit
is the hard part, because while it seems that our arguments against the design
of Ian are being heard, I don't think they are being _listened_ to.

-spongy

It doesn't take into account the fact that someone could try to use, if not All
his powers, at least a good majority of them. It's not that hard, if you don't
mind being rather contrived and warped in your thinking. There's that
Obfuscate, Dominate, Fortitude, Presence, Auspex Bleed monstrousity that I've
been theorizing about for a while, and Ian, although he'd only have 7 points for
eight, would be better than almost anyone, excepting, perhaps, Arika.

And beyond contrived tricks to break Ian(hey, that's how cards get broken almost
all the time...), there's the fact that he violates a basic game concept of
equitable costs for comparable vampires.

>telling the design team that some card they've designed is "wrong"?
>After much repitition of the same points, the fact is that the card has
>been printed and will be available for purchase in a matter of weeks.

It's tragic, really, that all our concerns have been disregarded. And even more
tragic if you want to have such utter faith in the design team, which is
composed of people just like us, that our arguments are ignored or passed off
as whining. The people who have been most vocal on this argument(which has been
going on for about a month now) are primarily the more respected and
longer-standing members of this newsgroup, and almost to a man, the consensus is
that Ian is vastly underpriced and a truly bad precedent to set.

>As people begin to play with the card, one of two things will happen: Ian
>will severely unbalance the game... or he won't. At that point, if you
>find that the card is broken, you have the power to add the "no Ian
>Forestal" house rule.

Sigh. Here we go again.

The point is not that Ian himself will massively unbalance the game on his
own(although he almost certainly would in a sealed enviroment like the
tournament I'm planning on running at halloween), but rather that he is
obscenely underpriced for the abilities which he is granted. Even assuming that
he pays normal price for his in-clan disciplines, he's getting 14 points of
disciplines for a two point special ability. Of this there is no question.

Now compare this to how much most other vampires pay for their disciplines and
special abilities, and you'll quickly see that Ian gets much more for his points
than ANYONE else. Where this on its own is not necessarily totally
unbalancing(although from a theoretical point of view it is...), it sets a truly
nasty precedent for some hypothetical WotC Tremere lover to create a vampire at
three capacity which has 14 points of disciplines, because, after all, Ian did
it... That is, of course, the most ridiculous example I could think up. But,
unfortunately, our ability to have faith in the design team has been shaken by
various other cards which violate basic game premises and have been observed to
be overpowered(Muaziz, Spiridonas...). If this trend continues, I would not be
(too) surprised to find a Tremere like that staring at me out of a booster of
the All-Tremere/Thaumaturgy expansion.

Signing off before he gets too vitriolic,

Alec Chang

After following this debate for the past month or so, I felt compelled
to offer my thoughts...

My worries about Ian are not so much that he is unbalancing, but that
he is unimaginative. By making a card of such a universal nature, he
spoils the interplay of clans that makes deck building such an interesting
challenge. IMHO, he is not that much more powerful than some of the
other vampires that have appeared in expansion sets.

I know little about the role-playing game associated with V:TeS, but
Ian seems a world away from what little I have seen. Much has been written
on the subject of game balance, and it seems to me that if V:TeS is based
loosely around some sort of mythos, it benefitted originally from keeping
to that. Hence the good overall balance of the original set, (with only a
few exceptions).

good spirit, and no long term offence has been caused. I agree that
much of the discussion is now moot, but I am sure there will be other

haven't got the expansions are not exactly going to be inspired

over here. (Witness the lack of UK posts on this group.)

About these points against the Toreador, where are you coming from.

Stealth - Tors don't have stealth, admitted, but Gangrels (Gans) don't
either (except for Backways) and the Gans voting sucks. Besides, with the
Grand Ball you don't need any stealth at all to get your equipment.

Combat - Tors have the option of blurring in combat, majestying out of it,
and seeing your opponents hand (one of the most useful and underplayed
cards in the game I feel is Aura Reading?)

Bleed - Their bleed is excellent. Its a natural trait for the Tors to
bleed at +1 and their presence abilities can add up to better bleeds than
most (Tremere, Malks and Vents excepted) and you still get some pool gain.

Vote - Only the Brujah and Vents can compare, and even they don't have the
dreaded Scorn of Adonis.

Toreadors are very versatile, they can bleed better than most, block
almost anything, and vote just about anything through. They lack some
stealth, but a few Cam Exemplarys, and Aching Beauty's fix that. Over all
they are much more useful overall than the other clans. True, if you want
to focus on a specific type of deck - Combat, Vote, etc., they are not the
clan, but if you want to focus on more than one type (some bleed with
political power). Besides, noone can go as defensive as the Tors.

To add my two cents:

I love the Toreador. They in my humble opinion make an excellent clan on
their own or as a backup clan in a two or three clan deck.

First let's look at the disciplines:

Presence: Superior bleed (3 direct bleed cards and Aire of elation to
boost the bleed much higher). Enchant Kindred at superior to get smaller
vamps out (I know there isn't any stealth on it but see below). Majesty
to fake out an opponent and tap his minions.

Celerity: My favorite of the combat disciplines. Potence, Thaumaturgy,
and Protean can all hit harder but what does it matter when you can't
actually touch me?

Auspex: The intercepting discipline. It also has Telepathic counter and
Telepathich Misdirection for any pesky bleeders.

Also several of the larger vamps have dominate to make the bleeding even
scarier.

Next let's look at the vampires:

The Toreadors got all my favorite abilities.

Anson: who can argue with two master cards a turn?

Masika: can you say "Energizer Bunny"?

Anneke: I annoyed one person to death with her ability to try and blcok
any action (he was my grand predator/great-grand prey). He couldn't get
out a piece of equipment if his life depended on it.

Francois Villon: Steal two blood as a +1 stealth action. I like it. How
about you?

Alexandra: Can untap and tap Toreadors. Francois twice (steal four blood
a round) is not a very nice sight.

Next, how about clan cards:

Toreador Grand Ball: Alexandra to make the tapped factor a non factor and
the intercept in the clan to make sure the card stays around. This card
is one of the most evil things I've seen. Now you don't get a chance to
block Francois. Those Enchant Kindreds ARE going to happen now.
Equipping is a joke now. Votes? Oh you were going to block. I'm sorry
but you can't!

Aching Beauty: Makes blocking just a little more painful

Art Museum: One of the 3 original clan feeders

The Portrait: Not a very useful card but weird enough that even a
Malkavian would love it.

Scorn of Adonis: It's a reverse bribes

The Louvre: Tap anyone? I like it, how about you? (I'm assuming Francois
or the Prince card is out there somewhere)

Finally as a back up clan:

Any voting deck can always use the Princes of the Toreadors (they have 5)
and the presence makes them an excellent compiment to the Ventrue.

Presence and Celerity overlap with the Brujah. 3 vampires also have
potence making the connenction even better. The auspex of the Toreador
can also be used for card intercept that the Brujah lack.

Toreador/Malkavian. The only reason I mention this one is the Masika
impersonating a Malk and getting the Madness Network out. On the other
hand the celerity and auspex do mesh nicely.

Toreador/Ravnos. On the surface this shouldn't work but there are two
Ravnos that have auspex and two that have celerity while Francois Villon
has chimestry (Toreador Grand Ball and Sensory Deprivations, nuff said).

Toreador/Tremer. I haven't actually tried this but once again the
celerity and auspex do overlap somewhat.

In closing I would like to point out that no clan is useless. I have seen
a Nosferatu deck pummel people into the ground (well he did get a good
draw and everyone else got crap but still.....), and I've seen Gangrel
decks win it all (and not with that infinite loop thing). I can say I've
definitely romped through many a methusaleh with a Toreador deck.

If you can't build a deck around the Toreador that doesn't mean they suck,
it just means that you don't have the cards to make them work or you're
biased against the Toreadors and have a subconsious will to see them do
badly.

Just my thoughts

Jeff Dai
